title: Trump-Xi summit: Who is competing?
gist: Sam Roggeveen argues the lavish pageantry of Xi Jinping's Washington summit, with Trump appearing deferential, belies US-China 'strategic competition'. Xi's call for 'healthy' competition is read as a bid for America to give way in Asia, and with thin US cultural ties to Asia, no ideological threat perception and no presidential framing of China as an enemy, the summit may signal the US granting China the status of equal.

insights.claim: At Xi Jinping's Washington visit, Trump appeared deferential to the point of obsequiousness, and his 'G2' framing makes it even less clear he sees China as a strategic competitor.
insights.speaker: Sam Roggeveen
insights.so_what: Points to US-China detente risk/upside, relevant for tariffs and tech controls.
insights.quote: he has appeared deferential to the point of obsequiousness
insights.locator: So elaborate has been the pageantry

insights.claim: The lasting impression of the summit may be that the US is prepared to grant China the status not of competitor but of equal.
insights.speaker: Sam Roggeveen
insights.so_what: A G2-style accommodation would reprice Asian geopolitical risk and US allies' positions.
insights.quote: perhaps the lasting impression formed by the summit will be that the United States is prepared to grant China the status not of competitor, but of equal
insights.locator: President Trump is the least likely

insights.claim: Xi said competition should be healthy, kept within bounds, and 'a race of catching up' rather than a wrestle with a winner and loser, effectively confining competition to positive-sum areas like technology and economics.
insights.speaker: Sam Roggeveen
insights.so_what: China seeks economic engagement while sidelining zero-sum strategic contests.
insights.quote: It should be a race of catching up with one another, not a wrestle in which one either wins or loses.
insights.locator: It was left to President Xi

insights.claim: Strategic competition over Taiwan and Asia Pacific leadership is inherently zero-sum: 'not a race, it's a boxing match'.
insights.speaker: Sam Roggeveen
insights.so_what: Taiwan risk cannot be resolved through economic competition framing.
insights.quote: Competition over Taiwan is not a race, it’s a boxing match.
insights.locator: In other words, Xi wants competition

insights.claim: Xi's remark is best read not as reluctance to compete but as wanting America to give in, since China, located in Asia, is more invested in the contest than the US.
insights.speaker: Sam Roggeveen
insights.so_what: Asymmetric resolve favours China over time in regional leadership.
insights.quote: the more plausible reading of Xi’s remark is that he wants America to give in

insights.claim: Both countries have ample capability, so the winner of strategic competition will be decided by will and resolve.
insights.speaker: Sam Roggeveen
insights.so_what: Political resolve, not military hardware, is the key variable to monitor.

insights.claim: Citing Dov Levin, Americans have thinner cultural and family ties to Asia than to Europe and do not see China as an ideological threat, unlike the Soviet Union during the Cold War.
insights.speaker: Sam Roggeveen
insights.so_what: Weak public motivation limits sustained US commitment in Asia.

insights.claim: China's economic power makes US elites differently disposed toward it; for example, it is financially risky for Hollywood studios to cast China as a villain.
insights.speaker: Sam Roggeveen
insights.so_what: Commercial exposure to China dampens US political will for confrontation.
insights.quote: it is financially risky for Hollywood film studios to make China a villain in their summer blockbusters

insights.claim: Unlike the Cold War or post-9/11, US-China competition has produced no comparable intellectual ferment in America, though the stakes are far higher.
insights.speaker: Sam Roggeveen
insights.so_what: Absence of an elite consensus undermines durability of hawkish China policy.
insights.locator: But those commercial pressures don’t apply

insights.claim: No recent president has spoken of China as an enemy, called it an 'evil empire' as Reagan did of the USSR, or proposed Truman-style global containment; Trump is the least likely to do so.
insights.speaker: Sam Roggeveen
insights.so_what: Rhetorical restraint suggests limited appetite for escalation under Trump.
insights.locator: At least part of the explanation
